When Dengue Mosquitoes "Ascend" to the Batu and Malang Highlands 
 PENYAKIT DAN IKLIM When Dengue Mosquitoes "Ascend" to the Batu and Malang Highlands
 Dengue fever continues to be reported in the highlands of Batu and Malang. While cooler temperatures help reduce cases, increased mobility among residents and the adaptability of mosquitoes maintain the risk of transmission.
 16 Nov 2026 07:00 WIB · Kesehatan 
 Kecil Sedang Besar Sangat Besar Share
 Copy Link
 By Defri Werdiono 
 This article has been translated using AI. See original . 
 00:00 00:00 10 10 1.00x The cooler highlands of Greater Malang, East Java, still allow dengue fever transmission, even though the Aedes aegypti mosquito prefers warmer temperatures. High levels of community mobility also contribute.
 Bambang (54), a resident of Batu City in East Java, initially believed that the fever and headaches experienced by his child, HF (15), in mid-October 2026 were symptoms of a common flu. However, after being rushed to Karsa Husada Regional General Hospital in Batu, doctors diagnosed his child with dengue fever.
 "Because at that time there was blood coming from his nose, a nosebleed, I immediately took him to the emergency room at Karsa Husada Regional Hospital. There, he received immediate treatment, including a check of his platelet count, which was 190 (190,000 per microliter of blood)," he said on Tuesday (10/11/2026).
 After receiving intensive treatment at the hospital, the patient's platelet count gradually rose to over 200,000 per microliter the following day. His condition continued to improve, and a week later, he was discharged.
 According to Bambang, he never suspected HF was infected with the dengue virus, which is transmitted through the Aedes aegypti mosquito. The initial signs didn't point to dengue fever, as he had previously believed. His child's appetite remained high.
 "Could the symptoms be different from the dengue fever we used to know? In dengue, as far as I know, there are spots on the arms. But there are none here," he said.
 Before being taken to the regional hospital, HF only complained of fever and dizziness. Bambang provided him with over-the-counter fever-reducing medication commonly available at pharmacies. However, the self-medication efforts proved ineffective, prompting Bambang to take HF to a primary healthcare facility located not far from their home.
 "When given fever-reducing medication, his body temperature decreased, but it rose again once the effects of the medication wore off. Initially, the doctor suspected typhus and prescribed several types of medication. If there is no improvement after three days, the doctor advised that he should be taken back to the healthcare facility," he said.
 Three days later, Bambang took his child back to the doctor. However, the complaints had not subsided, and eventually, the child experienced a nosebleed. Bambang was unsure when and where HF contracted dengue. His child had been active in various locations, and there were no known cases of dengue fever in their neighborhood.
 In Batu City, between January and October 2026, there were 96 cases of dengue fever and dengue shock syndrome (DSS) with no deaths. This figure is still lower than 2024, which recorded 444 cases and five deaths. Meanwhile, in 2023 and 2025, there were 128 and 164 cases, respectively, with one death in each year.
 The Head of the Batu City Health Office, Yuni Astuti, stated that the trend of dengue fever in Batu City is declining due to several factors, including intensified prevention efforts and mosquito breeding area eradication efforts. In addition, programs and cross-sector coordination are being strengthened to suppress the proliferation of Aedes aegypti.
 "Additionally, there has been an improvement in early detection and management of dengue fever at healthcare facilities. Community health centers and hospitals are becoming quicker and more responsive in identifying and treating patients from the outset, thereby reducing the rates of deterioration and mortality," he said.
 Despite being situated at an altitude of 800 to 2,000 meters above sea level, Yuni noted that the climate conditions in Batu still pose a risk for the spread of dengue fever. According to data from the Central Statistics Agency, the average temperature in Batu ranges from 15 to 19 degrees Celsius, with humidity levels generally between 75 and 98 percent.
 "Batu City's average elevation of 921 meters above sea level is not yet sufficiently protective. The average temperature in Batu City also still supports the breeding of the Aedes aegypti mosquito. High humidity prolongs the vector's survival. High rainfall also causes a lot of standing water," he said.
 Batu is one of the tourist cities in East Java, attracting a significant influx of visitors from outside the region. Notably, the number of tourists visiting Batu is expected to reach 9.7 million by 2025.
 According to Yuni, dengue fever cases in highland cities are influenced by several factors, including human mobility and movement. Immigrants and tourists experiencing viremia can carry the virus. Other factors include changes in land use, climate change, and rising temperatures in urban areas, or the microclimate.
 In addition, the Aedes aegypti mosquito has also adapted and developed resistance to insecticides.
 "If the symptoms of dengue fever are similar, they include sudden fever; headaches; pain behind the eyes; nausea and vomiting; muscle, bone, and joint pain; red rashes on the skin; and bleeding manifestations, such as nosebleeds and bleeding gums," he explained.
 Malang Regency 
 A similar situation is occurring in Malang Regency, where several areas border and share nearly the same elevation as Batu. One of these is Pujon District, located in the western mountainous region at an altitude of 1,100 to 1,200 meters above sea level, and Poncokusumo District in the eastern mountainous area, which ranges from 600 to 2,000 meters above sea level.
 In a separate interview, Titis Ari Respatilatsih, Head of the Disease Prevention and Control Division at the Malang District Health Office, stated that dengue fever also affects residents living in high-topography areas. However, compared to lowland regions, the number of dengue cases in highland areas is lower.
 According to data from the Malang District Health Office as of November 7, 2026, dengue fever cases have fluctuated throughout the year, with a peak occurring at the beginning of the year. From January to November 7, the cumulative total of dengue fever cases in Malang District reached 1,078, while the number of DBD cases stood at 581.
 The highest surge occurred in February 2026, with 145 dengue infection cases and 94 cases of dengue hemorrhagic fever (DBD). As the year progressed, the number of cases declined but began to rise again in September.
 "In early November, the number of cases was low, with only seven reported, but vigilance must remain heightened as increased rainfall could trigger mosquito breeding," said Titis.
 According to Titis, the three sub-districts with the highest number of dengue fever cases are Sumbermanjing Wetan with 41 cases, Turen with 41 cases, and Singosari with 36 cases. Meanwhile, when considering the total accumulation of dengue infections, ranging from mild to severe, Singosari ranks first with 97 cases, followed by Pakisaji with 71 cases and Sumbermanjing Wetan with 65 cases.
 Geographical factors and altitude, Titis continued, do influence differences in the number of dengue fever cases between regions or environmental epidemiology.
 Lowland areas are at higher risk. Aedes aegypti thrives in warm, densely populated areas with numerous standing water. Singosari, Turen, and Pakisaji share these characteristics, from warm temperatures to high community mobility, which increases the risk of transmission.
 In contrast, other areas such as Pujon and Ngantang report significantly lower case numbers. Pujon, for instance, has recorded only four cases. This region is situated in a highland area with cooler temperatures, which can hinder mosquito breeding and reduce their biting aggression.
 "However, the highlands are not completely immune, so absolute vigilance is necessary," he said.
 Anticipatory measures 
 The Batu City and Malang Regency governments have implemented several measures to curb the spread of dengue fever, particularly ahead of the rainy season. In Malang Regency, the strengthening of the mosquito breeding eradication program (PSN) through the 3M initiative is being carried out across 33 sub-districts down to the neighborhood level. The "one house, one jumantik" movement is also being promoted to enhance community independence in maintaining their local environments.
 "Engaging in community service for vector control is essential. Additionally, using lotion to prevent mosquito bites, which typically occur in the morning, is important. We must ensure there is no standing water, as this is crucial to interrupting mosquito breeding," he said.
 In addition, the Malang Regency Government is increasing public awareness and education. According to Titis, fogging is also carried out selectively based on standard operating procedures, including after laboratory results indicate positive dengue fever and through rigorous epidemiological investigations, such as the discovery of additional cases within a 100-200 meter radius and the presence of mosquito larvae.
 A similar approach has been taken by the Batu City Government. With a smaller area comprising three sub-districts, the local health department has implemented various measures to combat the issue, including providing laboratory support services for early detection of dengue fever at community health centers and enhancing surveillance and early reporting of cases from hospitals.
 Strengthening programs and cross-sector coordination is also underway. "We are enhancing the PSN plus movement with a letter urging the public to be vigilant about dengue fever. This includes health promotion, dengue education, and encouraging clean and healthy living practices among the community," Yuni stated.
